title: What are the JVM memory areas — Heap (objects, shared across threads: Young Gen + Old Gen), Stack (per thread: local variables, method calls), Metaspace (class metadata, replaces PermGen in Java 8+), Code Cache (JIT-compiled native code)?
shortTitle: What are the JVM memory areas?
topicTitle: What are the JVM memory areas

s1_definition.profdef: The JVM divides runtime memory into distinct regions, each with a specific job. The Heap holds all objects and is shared across every thread, and it is internally split into the Young Generation (newly created objects) and the Old Generation (long-lived objects). Each thread gets its own Stack holding local variables and method call frames. Metaspace (which replaced PermGen in Java 8) stores class metadata in native memory. The Code Cache stores native machine code produced by the Just-In-Time compiler.

Inside the vault there is a fast-moving front shelf for today's cash (Young Generation) and a deep storage room for old deposits (Old Generation). Each teller like Rajesh has his own private desk drawer (Stack) for the forms he is working on right now. The rulebook that describes what an "Account" even is sits in the manager's office (Metaspace). And the bank's shortcut cheat-sheets for the fastest common operations are pinned on the wall (Code Cache).

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The JVM divides runtime memory into distinct regions, each with a specific job. The Heap holds all objects and is shared across every thread, and it is internally split into the Young Generation (newly created objects) and the Old Generation (long-lived objects). Each thread gets its own Stack holding local variables and method call frames. Metaspace (which replaced PermGen in Java 8) stores class metadata in native memory. The Code Cache stores native machine code produced by the Just-In-Time compiler.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India as a building. The Heap is the big shared vault where all the money objects (accounts, transactions) are kept, and every teller can reach it. Inside the vault there is a fast-moving front shelf for today's cash (Young Generation) and a deep storage room for old deposits (Old Generation). Each teller like Rajesh has his own private desk drawer (Stack) for the forms he is working on right now. The rulebook that describes what an "Account" even is sits in the manager's office (Metaspace). And the bank's shortcut cheat-sheets for the fastest common operations are pinned on the wall (Code Cache).

**One line to remember:** Heap is shared objects, Stack is per-thread locals, Metaspace is class blueprints, Code Cache is compiled native code.

sections.s2_technical:
The Heap is the largest memory region and the only place where objects live. When you write `new Account("SAV2001")`, the JVM allocates that object on the heap. Because the heap is shared by all threads, it is the region the garbage collector manages. The heap is split into the Young Generation and the Old Generation. The Young Generation itself has three parts: Eden (where brand-new objects are born) and two Survivor spaces called S0 and S1. Objects that keep surviving garbage collections eventually get promoted into the Old Generation.

Each thread has its own Stack. Every time a method is called, a new stack frame is pushed holding that method's local variables, parameters, and the return address. For example, when `transfer()` calls `debit()`, a frame for `debit()` is pushed on top. When `debit()` returns, its frame is popped. Primitive locals like `int count` live directly on the stack, while object references on the stack point to objects on the heap: `Account rajesh = new Account(...)` puts the reference `rajesh` on the stack and the actual object on the heap. If recursion goes too deep, the stack overflows and you get a `StackOverflowError`.

Metaspace stores class metadata — the structure of each loaded class, method bytecode, and the runtime constant pool. Before Java 8 this lived in a fixed-size region called PermGen inside the heap, which frequently caused `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space`. Java 8 moved it to native memory and renamed it Metaspace, which grows automatically but can be capped with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`.

The Code Cache holds native machine code generated by the JIT compiler. When a method becomes "hot" (called many times), the JIT compiles it from bytecode to native code and stores it here so future calls skip interpretation. If the Code Cache fills up, the JIT stops compiling and performance degrades.

A senior-level nuance: the Program Counter register and native method stacks are also per-thread JVM areas, but the four regions above are what matter most in interviews and tuning.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the transfer service creates thousands of short-lived objects per second: request DTOs, temporary `BigDecimal` amounts, validation results. These objects are born and die almost immediately. This is exactly how the Young Generation works — most objects die young, so they are created in Eden and cleaned up quickly without touching the rest of memory.

Problem 2 — A few objects, like the long-running connection pool and cached account lookups, must survive for hours. This is exactly how the Old Generation works — objects that survive several collections get promoted there and are collected rarely.

Problem 3 — When Rajesh's `transfer()` method calls `debit()` and `credit()`, each call needs its own private workspace for its local variables so the calls do not interfere. This is exactly what the Stack provides — one frame per method call, per thread.

Our mini-project builds a small `MemoryDemo` that creates account objects (heap), runs nested method calls (stack frames), and prints the live memory regions using the `Runtime` and `MemoryMXBean` APIs so the reader can SEE each region. The classes are: an `Account` domain object, a `TransferService` with nested method calls, and a `MemoryInspector` that reports heap, non-heap (Metaspace), and thread stack usage.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jvm-memory-demo/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/
            ├── MemoryDemo.java            (main runnable demo)
            ├── Account.java               (heap object)
            ├── TransferService.java       (nested stack frames)
            └── MemoryInspector.java       (reports memory regions)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/jvm/*.java

# Run and watch the heap grow and shrink
java -Xms64m -Xmx256m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=128m \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.MemoryDemo

# Print GC activity so you can SEE Young/Old collections
java -Xms64m -Xmx256m -Xlog:gc -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.MemoryDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two accounts (Rajesh SAV2001 with 1,000,000 rupees, Priya CUR3001 with 250,000 rupees) and a transfer of 50,000 rupees.

Step 1 — The JVM starts. Class metadata for `Account`, `TransferService`, and `MemoryDemo` is loaded into Metaspace (native memory). The bytecode and field layout for each class lives here.

Step 2 — `main()` begins. A stack frame for `main` is pushed onto the main thread's Stack. The local reference variables `rajesh`, `priya`, `inspector` live in this frame.

Step 3 — `new Account(...)` runs twice. Two Account objects are allocated in Eden inside the Young Generation on the Heap. The stack holds only the references; the actual objects live on the heap.

Step 4 — The loop creates 100,000 temporary strings in Eden. Eden fills up, triggering Minor GC. Survivors move to a Survivor space; the rest are reclaimed. After `clear()`, the strings become unreachable and are collected on the next Minor GC.

Step 5 — `service.transfer(...)` is called. A `transfer` frame is pushed. Inside it, `debit()` is called, pushing a `debit` frame on top. When `debit()` returns, its frame is popped. Then `credit()` is called and popped. Balances on the heap objects change: Rajesh 1,000,000 becomes 950,000, Priya 250,000 becomes 300,000.

Step 6 — The `MemoryInspector` reads live heap and non-heap usage from `Runtime` and `MemoryMXBean` and logs each region.

Final output:

```
2026-10-31 22:50:01 [INFO] Created heap objects: SAV2001, CUR3001
2026-10-31 22:50:01 [INFO] After creating 2 accounts -> Heap used=8MB / max=256MB | NonHeap(Metaspace+CodeCache)=14MB
2026-10-31 22:50:01 [INFO] After creating & releasing 100k temp objects -> Heap used=11MB / max=256MB | NonHeap=15MB
2026-10-31 22:50:01 [INFO] Transfer of 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 complete
2026-10-31 22:50:01 [INFO] After transfer -> Heap used=9MB / max=256MB | NonHeap=15MB
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  JVM Process starts
    │
    ▼
  Metaspace (native)            ← class blueprints loaded
    │  Account.class, TransferService.class metadata
    ▼
  main() thread STARTS
    │
    ├─ STACK (main thread)                 ├─ HEAP (shared)
    │  frame: main()                       │  Young Gen (Eden)
    │   ref rajesh ───────────────────────▶│   Account SAV2001 {bal:1,000,000}
    │   ref priya  ───────────────────────▶│   Account CUR3001 {bal:250,000}
    │  frame: transfer()                    │   100k temp strings → Minor GC → freed
    │   frame: debit()  (pushed/popped)     │
    │   frame: credit() (pushed/popped)     │  SAV2001 bal:1,000,000 → 950,000
    │                                       │  CUR3001 bal:250,000 → 300,000
    ▼                                       ▼
  CODE CACHE ← JIT compiles hot transfer()/debit() to native code
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM organizes runtime memory into four main areas, each with a clear purpose. The Heap is where every object lives and it is shared by all threads, which is why it is the region the garbage collector manages. The Heap is divided into the Young Generation, where new objects are born, and the Old Generation, where long-lived objects are promoted after surviving several collections. Each thread has its own Stack that holds method call frames with their local variables and parameters, which is why one thread's locals can never be seen by another thread. Metaspace, which replaced PermGen in Java 8 and now lives in native memory, holds class metadata like field layouts and method bytecode. The Code Cache holds the native machine code that the Just-In-Time compiler produces for hot methods.

Understanding this split matters because it tells you where a memory problem comes from. If the Heap fills up you get an OutOfMemoryError in heap space and you take a heap dump. If Metaspace fills up, usually from a class-loading leak, you get an OutOfMemoryError in Metaspace. If recursion runs away you get a StackOverflowError on the thread stack. Each symptom points to a different region and a different fix.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this knowledge is practical every day. Our transfer service creates huge numbers of short-lived request objects that are born and die in the Young Generation, so Minor GC handles them cheaply and frequently. A handful of long-lived objects like the connection pool get promoted to the Old Generation and are collected rarely. When we had a memory issue, knowing the regions let me immediately decide whether to take a heap dump for the Heap or inspect class loading for Metaspace, instead of guessing. That is why I always tune `-Xms` and `-Xmx` for the Heap and watch non-heap memory separately in production.
